title: Realization of Arbitrary Gauge Fields via Symmetry-Protected Zero Modes
authors: J. X. Dai, Bingbing Wang, Jiangzi Chen, Y. X. Zhao, Haoran Xue
abstract: Gauge fields are fundamental to modern physics, but prescribed gauge configurations are often difficult to implement in artificial systems. Here, we present a general scheme for realizing arbitrary static $\mathrm{O}(N)$ lattice gauge configurations using symmetry-protected zero modes of sublattice-imbalanced bipartite units. The target $\mathrm{O}(N)$ link on each bond is encoded in the connectivity and strengths of positive microscopic couplings. By decoupling the zero-mode manifold from the remaining modes, the target gauge Hamiltonian forms an exact spectral block of the microscopic tight-binding model rather than a perturbative approximation. We experimentally demonstrate this framework in acoustic crystals through a $\mathbb{Z}_2$ quadrupole topological insulator, an $\mathrm{SO}(2)$ Hofstadter model, and an $\mathrm{SO}(3)$ non-Abelian topological insulator. Our results provide a general and accessible route to gauge-field physics in artificial systems.
summary: The paper introduces a general and highly robust method to engineer arbitrary static O(N) lattice gauge fields in artificial systems. By exploiting symmetry-protected zero modes within bipartite units, the authors ensure that the target Hamiltonian is realized exactly, avoiding perturbative errors. This technique has been experimentally validated using acoustic resonators for realizing $\mathbb{Z}_2$, SO(2), and SO(3) topological models.
main_problem: The primary challenge addressed is realizing arbitrary static O(N) lattice gauge configurations within artificial physical systems.
main_result: The authors present a general scheme that achieves this by encoding the target gauge field into the symmetry-protected zero modes of sublattice-imbalanced bipartite units, demonstrated successfully across multiple topological models.
method: The methodology involves constructing an effective Hamiltonian ($	ext{H}_{	ext{eff}}$) by projecting the microscopic tight-binding model onto the zero-mode subspace, ensuring this projection is an exact spectral block rather than a perturbative approximation.
model_or_system: The framework is demonstrated using acoustic crystals (coupled resonators), realizing specific models like a $\mathbb{Z}_2$ quadrupole topological insulator, an SO(2) Hofstadter model, and an SO(3) non-Abelian topological insulator.
key_observables: Transmission spectra, energy/frequency spectra of bulk/edge states, and field localization at boundaries are used as key diagnostic observables.
important_parameters: The construction relies on using only positive microscopic couplings (for experimental feasibility), and requires a sufficiently large intra-unit gap to isolate the zero-mode subspace.
main_assumptions: The method assumes that all necessary physical couplings can be realized as positive real numbers, allowing for mapping continuous gauge fields onto discrete artificial atom couplings.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the general framework of using a three-site unit to create an O(N) artificial atom. Specific applications show the realization of edge states and flux patterns in acoustic resonators for the $\mathbb{Z}_2$ TI, SO(2) model, and SO(3) insulator.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the theoretical zero-mode construction using bipartite units, details the general procedure for projecting to an exact gauge Hamiltonian, and then presents experimental demonstrations across three distinct physical realizations ($\mathbb{Z}_2$, SO(2), SO(3)).
why_interesting: This work provides a powerful, experimentally accessible blueprint for engineering complex quantum Hamiltonians—specifically those containing non-trivial gauge fields—using only local interactions in platforms like acoustics or photonics.
